source_text: Quos imitantur scilicet atque sectantur qui, Dei traditione contempta, alienas doctrinas appetunt et magisteria humanae institutionis inducunt; quos increpat Dominus et objurgat in Evangelio suo dicens: Rejicitis mandatum Dei, ut traditionem vestram statuatis. Pejus hoc crimen est quam quod admisisse lapsi videntur; qui tamen in poenitentia criminis constituti Deum plenis satisfactionibus deprecantur. Hic Ecclesia quaeritur et rogatur, illic Ecclesiae repugnatur. Hic potest necessitas fuisse, illic voluntas tenetur in scelere. Hic qui lapsus est sibi tantum nocuit, illic qui haeresim vel schisma facere conatus est multos secum trahendo decepit. Hic animae unius est damnum, illic periculum plurimorum. Certe peccasse se hic et intelligit, et lamentatur et plangit; ille tumens in pectore suo, et in ipsis sibi delictis placens, a matre filios segregat, oves a pastore sollicitat, Dei sacramenta disturbat: et cum lapsus semel peccaverit, ille quotidie peccat. Postremo lapsus, martyrium postmodum consecutus, potest regni promissa percipere; ille, si extra Ecclesiam fuerit occisus, ad Ecclesiae non potest praemia pervenire.
pass_a_gloss: Those, of course, are imitated and followed by who, having despised God's tradition, desire alien doctrines and introduce human institutions of magisterium; who the Lord reproaches and rebukes in His Gospel, saying: You reject the command of God, so that you may establish your tradition. This crime is worse than that which the lapsed seem to have committed; who, however, having been established in penitence of the crime, pray to God with full satisfactions. Here the Church is sought and asked, there the Church is resisted. Here necessity may have been, there the will is held in crime. Here he who has lapsed has harmed only himself, there he who has attempted to make heresy or schism, having deceived many by drawing them with himself. Here the loss is of one soul, there the danger is of many. Certainly, he here has sinned and understands it, and laments and mourns; that one, swelling in his own breast, and pleasing himself in his own delicts, separates sons from their mother, solicits sheep from the shepherd, disturbs God's sacraments: and when the lapsed has sinned once, that one sins daily. Finally, the lapsed, having afterwards attained martyrdom, can receive the promises of the kingdom; that one, if he has been killed outside the Church, cannot arrive at the rewards of the Church.

pass_b_english: Those who despise God's tradition, chase after alien doctrines, and introduce human teachings as their authority are precisely the ones who imitate and follow such men. The Lord reproaches and rebukes them in His Gospel, saying, "You reject the command of God, so that you may establish your own tradition" (Mark 7:9). This crime is worse than the sin the lapsed appear to have committed; those, though established in penance for their crime, pray to God with full satisfaction. Here the Church is sought and entreated; there the Church is resisted. Here necessity may have been the cause; there the will is held fast in wickedness. The one who lapsed harmed only himself; the one who attempts heresy or schism deceives many by drawing them along with him. Here the loss is of a single soul; there the danger threatens many. The lapsed man certainly knows he has sinned, and he laments and mourns; the other swells with pride in his own breast, takes pleasure in his own offenses, separates children from their mother, lures sheep away from the shepherd, and disrupts God's sacraments. When the lapsed man sins once, that one sins daily. Finally, the lapsed man, if he later attains martyrdom, can receive the promises of the kingdom; but the other, if killed outside the Church, cannot attain the Church's rewards.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the distinctions between the 'lapsed' (lapsi) and the 'heretic/schismatic' (ille/quo) made throughout the paragraph. Pass A preserves the syntax of the Latin, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that maintains the theological nuances (e.g., 'necessitas' vs 'voluntas', 'animae unius' vs 'plurimorum'). The scripture citation (Mark 7:9) correctly identifies the allusion in 'Rejicitis mandatum Dei, ut traditionem vestram statuatis'.
